items.title: Touching the Elephant – TPUs
items.raw_content: Something New There is mythological reverence for Google’s Tensor Processing Unit. While the world presently watches NVIDIA’s gravity drag more companies into its orbit, there sits Google, imperial and singular. Lots of companies participate in the “Cambrian-style explosion of new-interesting accelerators” [14] – Groq, Amazon, and Tenstorrent come to mind – but the TPU is the original existence proof. NVIDIA should take credit for the reemergence of deep learning, but the GPU wasn’t designed with deep learning in mind. What’s strange is that the TPU isn’t a secret. This research is indebted to Google’s public chest-thumping, but the devices themselves have long been exclusive to Google’s datacenters. That is over a decade of work on a hardware system sequestered behind their walls. That the TPU is so well documented yet without a true counterpart creates a strange asymmetry. Google is we
items.summary: An essay examines Google's Tensor Processing Unit as the original proof that purpose-built AI accelerators work, noting the chips have long been confined to Google's datacenters despite extensive public documentation.

So what has transpired since? The updates in this section are in reverse chronological order (newest on top) Fisher-Price (owned by Mattel) produced some toys in the early 2000 under the Pixter brand. items.title: Tiny Core Linux: a 23 MB Linux distro with graphical desktop
items.raw_content: The Core Project is a highly modular based system with community build extensions. It starts with a recent Linux kernel, vmlinuz, and our root filesystem and start-up scripts packaged with a basic set of kernel modules in core.gz. Core (11MB) is simply the kernel + core.gz - this is the foundation for user created desktops, servers, or appliances. TinyCore is Core + Xvesa.tcz + Xprogs.tcz + aterm.tcz + fltk-1.3.tcz + flwm.tcz + wbar.tcz TinyCore becomes simply an example of what the Core Project can produce, an 16MB FLTK/FLWM desktop. CorePlus ofers a simple way to get started using the Core philosophy with its included community packaged extensions enabling easy embedded frugal or pendrive installation of the user's choice of supported desktop, while maintaining the Core principal of mounted extensions with full package management. It is not a complete desktop nor is all hardware comple
items.title_zh: Tiny Core Linux：23 MB 的图形桌面 Linux 发行版
items.summary: Tiny Core Linux is a highly modular distribution built from a recent Linux kernel and a small core filesystem, with TinyCore adding a lightweight FLTK/FLWM graphical desktop.

items.title: HTML as an Accessible Format for Papers (2023)
items.raw_content: Accessibility barriers in research are not new, but they are urgent. The message we have heard from our community is that arXiv can have the most impact in the shortest time by offering HTML papers alongside the existing PDF. arXiv has successfully launched papers in HTML format. We are gradually backfilling HTML for arXiv's corpus of over 2 million papers over time. Not every paper can be successfully converted, so a small percentage of papers will not have an HTML version. We will work to improve conversion over time.
items.title_zh: HTML 作为论文的可访问格式（2023）
items.summary: arXiv says it now offers HTML versions of papers alongside PDFs to improve accessibility and is gradually backfilling HTML for a corpus of over 2 million papers; a small percentage cannot be converted.

items.title: Perl's decline was cultural
items.raw_content: There's been a flurry of discussion on Hacker News and other tech forums about what killed Perl. I wrote a lot of Perl in the mid 90s and subsequently worked on some of the most trafficked sites on the web in mod_perl in the early 2000s, so I have some thoughts. My take: it was mostly baked into the culture. Perl grew amongst a reactionary community with conservative values, which prevented it from evolving into a mature general purpose language ecosystem. Everything else filled the gap. Something to keep in mind, is that although this is my personal take, and therefore entirely an opinion piece, I was there at the time. I stopped doing Perl properly when I left Amazon, I think this would have been around 2005. It's based on the first hand impressions of somebody who was very deeply involved in Perl in its heyday, and moved on. I have a lot of experience, from both inside and outside the
items.title_zh: Perl 的衰落是文化原因
items.summary: A first-hand essay argues that Perl's decline was mainly cultural, saying its conservative community values kept it from evolving into a mature general-purpose language ecosystem.

items.title: Screenshots from developers: 2002 vs. 2015 (2015)

I recently republished them , and, seeing the interest this generated, I thought it’d be fun to ask the same people* again 13 years later. To my delight I managed to reach many of them. my desktop is pretty boring, since it consists of xterm windows to whatever unix system i am using at the moment. the machine itself is likely to be running some x-window server like exceed on some flavor of windows, though for many years i just used an x terminal.
